habitat: Blue cranes are endemic to southern Africa, with the vast majority of the population found in South Africa and small populations in Namibia and western Lesotho. They inhabit dry, open grasslands, semi-desert scrub, agricultural lands, and occasionally wetlands. Unlike most crane species, they are not strongly dependent on wetlands, having adapted to the drier grassland ecosystems of the highveld and Karoo. They have benefited somewhat from agriculture, foraging in grain fields and pastures, and are South Africa's national bird.
diet: Blue cranes are omnivorous foragers, feeding on seeds, grains, roots, tubers, insects (especially grasshoppers, caterpillars, and beetles), small reptiles, and occasionally fish. They forage primarily on the ground in open grasslands and agricultural fields, often in flocks of 10-100. In farming areas, they consume waste grain, maize, and wheat — which has helped sustain populations but also brings them into conflict with farmers. Their long, probing beaks allow them to extract food from grass tufts and shallow soil.
behavior: Blue cranes are social birds, gathering in large flocks of 100-1,000 individuals outside the breeding season — one of the largest crane congregations. During breeding, pairs separate to establish nesting territories. Their courtship displays are among the most elaborate of any crane species, involving synchronized dancing, leaping, wing-flapping, and tossing of grass and feathers into the air. Pairs mate for life. They nest on the ground in shallow scrapes, typically in grassland near water, laying 2 eggs. Both parents incubate and care for the chicks, which can walk shortly after hatching.
facts: The blue crane is South Africa's national bird and appears on the country's five-cent coin. It is the most range-restricted crane species, found almost entirely within South Africa. They have a distinctive blue-gray plumage that is pale and ethereal, with exceptionally long, flowing tertial feathers that nearly touch the ground — giving them an elegant, elongated silhouette. They are one of the smallest crane species at 100-120 centimeters tall. The species is classified as Vulnerable, with an estimated 25,000 remaining. Primary threats include habitat loss, agricultural pesticides, and power line collisions.
naming: Blue crane names might reflect their ethereal coloring, elegant dancing, or South African heritage. Consider names like Azure, Sky, Dance, Feather, Grace, Indigo, Zulu, Karoo, Velvet (for their soft plumage), Cirrus (like a wispy cloud), Sapphire, Ballerina, Kibo (African peak), or Thula (peace in Zulu).
